items.question: How does DeepWalk generalize neural language models, and what kind of output does DeepWalk produce when given a graph as input?
items.gold_answer: DeepWalk generalizes neural language models by applying them to a special language made of randomly generated walks. Given a graph as input, DeepWalk produces a latent representation as output.
items.evidence_quote: DeepW alkgeneralizes neural language models to process a special language composed of a set of randomly-generated walks.

items.question: What relationship does DeepWalk report between the 2-dimensional latent representation of the Karate network and the structure of the original graph?
items.gold_answer: The 2-dimensional embedding of the Karate network is strikingly similar to the force-directed visualization of the graph. DeepWalk also notes that linearly separable regions in the embedding correspond to clusters found by modularity maximization in the original graph.
items.evidence_quote: Beyond the striking similarity, we note that linearly separable portions of (1b) correspond to clusters found through modularity maximization in the input graph (1a) (shown as vertex colors).

items.question: Under which conditions does DeepWalk outperform other latent representation methods for creating social dimensions, according to the passage?
items.gold_answer: DeepWalk outperforms other latent representation methods especially when labeled nodes are scarce. The passage emphasizes that this advantage comes from learning label-independent graph representations.
items.evidence_quote: DeepW alkoutperforms other latent representation methods for creating social dimensions [39, 41], especially when labeled nodes are scarce.

items.question: Why can DeepWalk’s learned representations be shared among tasks, and what kind of classifier can achieve strong performance with them?
items.gold_answer: DeepWalk’s representations can be shared among tasks because their quality is not influenced by which vertices are labeled, since the method learns label-independent representations of the graph. The passage says that strong performance is possible with very simple linear classifiers such as logistic regression.
items.evidence_quote: Our representation quality is not influenced by the choice of labeled vertices, so they can be shared among tasks.
